name: Nectarines
why_now: Nectarines are peaches without the fuzz, and in August they often hit their stride as peach season winds down. The flavor is similar — sweet, aromatic, deeply summery — but the skin is thinner and doesn't need peeling. This is the last good stone fruit window before fall. It is also the month when the fruit has traveled the furthest and been kept the coldest, which is why choosing well matters more now than it did in July.
how_to_choose: Look at the background color, not the red blush — the gold or cream under the blush should have no green left in it. Red is variety and sun exposure, and it tells you nothing
Press the shoulder near the stem, not the cheek. The skin is thin enough to feel soft over flesh that isn't
Heavy for its size. A light nectarine was picked before it filled out
Buy from an unrefrigerated display when the store has one. Stone fruit chilled while still firm turns mealy and never recovers
Fragrance confirms; it doesn't filter. Cold fruit doesn't smell like anything, so a quiet nectarine with gold shoulders is still worth taking home
Avoid green shoulders and rock-hard fruit — that one was picked too early and will only soften, never sweeten
buy_this_much: 4–5 nectarines for the week. They don't all need to be ready on the same day.
buying_note: Firm is fine. Green is not. Take home nectarines that are heavy and gold-shouldered even if they don't give yet, then leave them on the counter for two or three days — stem side down, out of direct sun, in a paper bag if you want to hurry them. They will soften, get juicy, and start to smell like something. What they will not do is get sweeter than the day they were picked, which is why the color under the blush decides the purchase and the give only decides the day you eat it.
price_note: Stone fruit is still affordable in August, though supply thins by late in the month and more of it arrives from further away. Buy them when you see good ones — the window doesn't come back.

flavor_paths.name: Nearly nothing
flavor_paths.description: Sliced and eaten as they are. A pinch of flaky salt if you want to push it.

flavor_paths.name: With yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Sliced on Greek yogurt in the morning, maybe a little honey. That's it.

flavor_paths.name: On the plate
flavor_paths.description: Alongside burrata when figs aren't enough or aren't available.

weekday_uses: Sliced on Greek yogurt in the morning
Sliced alongside the weekend cheese plate
weekend_use: Alongside the fig and burrata plate — or in place of figs if they weren't available. The combination of ripe stone fruit, good cheese, and cured meat holds up in either direction.
storage: Counter until ripe, stem side down, in a single layer. Refrigerate only once it's fully soft and fragrant, and eat within a day or two after that. A firm nectarine put in the refrigerator is the one that comes out dry and cottony.
one_thing_to_learn: The dry, cottony nectarine has a name: internal breakdown, or woolliness. It happens when stone fruit is held cold — roughly 36°F to 46°F — while it is still firm, which describes almost every refrigerated grocery display in the second half of summer. The damage is done before you get there and cannot be undone on your counter. This is the whole reason a nectarine bought in August can look flawless, feel perfect, and taste like nothing. Buy from the room-temperature stack when there is one, ripen at home, and refrigerate only at the end.
